August 9 is

 International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples

 (August 9). Every day, we honor the sovereignty, richness, and beauty of Indigenous Peoples, languages, and lifeways.




The first meeting of the

 United Nations Working Group on Indigenous Populations

 was held in Geneva, Switzerland, on August 9, 1982. Since then, many spaces have opened up for Indigenous voices to be heard, and new agreements protecting the rights of Indigenous Peoples have been adopted. While we celebrate these outcomes, we also recognize that the promise of human rights for Indigenous Peoples worldwide remains unfulfilled. In many parts of the world, Indigenous Peoples are still facing grave human rights abuses and challenges.





This year's theme is 

“Honouring Indigenous Midwives: Safeguarding Life and Well-being.”




Indigenous Peoples, our values, and knowledge systems hold solutions to today’s greatest challenges, including climate change, ecocide, and biodiversity loss. content:
Former Indigenous authorities of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán released in Guatemala after more than a year in pretrial detention







Country

diana




Wed, 08/05/2026 - 22:19










Issues







Human Rights













Program







5













Main Image







 













Guatemala City, August 5, 2026.

 Luis Pacheco and Héctor Chaclán (both of Maya K'iche' origin), former president and former treasurer of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán, regained their freedom this Wednesday after being held since April 25, 2025 in the Mariscal Zavala prison. A judge granted them alternative measures to pretrial detention, allowing them to face the rest of the criminal proceedings outside of prison.




Both leaders had been prosecuted for illicit association, terrorism, and obstruction of justice, stemming from their leadership role in the 2023 protests in defense of that year's election results, when the Public Prosecutor's Office attempted to annul them over fraud allegations against the winning party.




The case against Pacheco and Chaclán was driven by the Public Prosecutor's Office, then headed by former Attorney General Consuelo Porras, together with the Special Prosecutor's Office Against Impunity, previously led by Rafael Curruchiche. By Dev Kumar Sunuwar

 (Koĩts-Sunuwar, CS Staff)




Standing as an Indigenous journalist among more than 400 fellow Indigenous-led media professionals, reporters, broadcasters, storytellers, Indigenous media scholars, and press-freedom advocates from July 22-24, 2026, I felt a sense of belonging and a pride in reclaiming our narratives. An annual gathering, organized by the Indigenous Journalists Association (IJA) and the Indigenous Media Conference 2026 in Portland, OR, brought together Indigenous media delegates from across the United States, Canada, Australia, and the Pacific Islands. For Indigenous storytellers and media professionals who have spent decades defending the truth, the conference made a clear message: reclaiming story ownership is important for our cultural, economic, political, and environmental survival. 




Observing and experiencing this conference firsthand, amid the worsening climate crisis, rapid expansion and changes in artificial intelligence, and increased threats for Indigenous journalists on the ground, was transformative. How Dignity and Resistance of the Maya Tz’utujil Peoples Triumphed over Corruption







Country

Program







5













Main Image







 













By Kerstin Sabene




On July 2, 2026, I boarded a 

lancha

, a small public boat from Panajachel to the Maya Tz'utujil village of Santiago on Lake Atitlan in Guatemala, which has been the site of heightened tensions since the beginning of the year. 




On October 24, 2025, the people of Santiago Atitlan succeeded in removing Mayor Francisco Coché Pablo from office on corruption charges. They forced his ouster following accusations of corruption regarding the illegal authorization of motor taxi licenses and a failure to respond to demands from ancestral authorities. They also succeeded in having the Supreme Electoral Tribunal recognize First Councilman Andrés Ajuchán Coó  as the new mayor. 




In February 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Coché's favor, and he was technically reinstated with a provisional authorization to return to his post. Guatemala’s judicial system is highly corrupt, and the court’s ruling by no means implies that the charges against Coché were invalid or that he was exonerated. title: The Price of Gold: The Xingu River and the Communities Facing Destruction
content:
The Price of Gold: The Xingu River and the Communities Facing Destruction







Country







Brazil










agnes




Tue, 07/28/2026 - 10:50










Issues







Human Rights













Program







5













Main Image







 













By Angel Ferreira 

(Payayá, CS Intern)




At Volta Grande do Xingu, Brazil, two Indigenous communities, the Arara da Volta Grande and the Yudjá, continue to defend their ancestral territories against mounting external pressures. For the Yudjá, their name carries profound significance: it affirms their sovereignty and enduring relationship with the Xingu River, a bond that shapes their identity, culture, and way of life.




Today, however, their traditional livelihoods face a severe threat. The Volta Grande Project, backed by an estimated $229 million investment from Belo Sun Mineração Ltda., a subsidiary of Belo Sun Mining Corp., aims to establish one of the largest open-pit gold mines in the region. Community leaders and environmental experts warn that the project could inflict irreversible damage on a river system already deeply destabilized by the Belo Monte Hydroelectric Dam.




To understand the technical, social, and legal dimensions of this ongoing struggle, Cultural Survival spoke with anthropologist Thais Mantovanelli from the Instituto Socioambiental (ISA) / Xingu Program.

These markets offer a unique opportunity for the public to meet Indigenous artists from around the world and to learn about different ways of seeing and being in this world.




At the Cultural Survival Bazaar on 

August 1-2, 2026, at Farm Fresh Providence

By Emily Pahuamba

 (CS Intern)




For generations, Indigenous Peoples have sustained their communities through ancestral knowledge passed down from one generation to the next. Through Cultural Survival's Indigenous Youth Fellowship Program, young leaders are preserving traditional medicine in Mexico, restoring ecological knowledge in Ecuador, and documenting cultural history and agricultural practices in Indonesia. Their work demonstrates that protecting ancestral knowledge is not only about honoring the past; it is about strengthening Indigenous identity, resilience, and self-determination for future generations.


 







 




Colectivo U Chak Lu'umil Ch'e'eno'ob, Mexico

 




In the Maya community of Kancabchén, Quintana Roo, Mexico, the U Chak Lu'umil Ch'e'eno'ob Collective (Red Land of Wells) comprises Yeni Tun, Brenda Pech, Doris Tun, and their coordinator, Nelly Cauich. All of them grew up in the community, and some later attended the Intercultural Maya University of Quintana Roo. By Phoebe Farris

 (Powhatan-Pamunkey) 




Faisu Mukunana (Tsou) is an acclaimed Indigenous woman writer from Taiwan. Born in the community of Lalauya in 1942, Mukunana has lived through two regimes: the Japanese occupation and the Republic of China. She speaks three languages, including her native Tsou, and is the recipient of several literary awards. 




Yao-Chung Tsao has a Ph.D. in Cognitive Psychology and a master’s degree in Industrial Engineering. Dr. Tsao has translated many books between Chinese and English, including Mukunana’s work, “My Dear Ak’i, Please Don’t Be Upset.”  He served on the faculty of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute before joining Bell Labs. Now retired, he focuses on writing, translating, and painting. I recently spoke with Dr. Tsao.

The Indigenous Community Media Fund

This fund was created to support initiatives by Indigenous organizations, collectives, and media outlets that contribute to strengthening their right to freedom of expression and access to information. Through these initiatives, we promote community awareness and organization around their worldviews, the defense of their rights, and their relationship with their territories.
